" <p> Menounos added that the darkening provides unhelpful feedback in a warming climate that will allow high melt rates to continue . <p> Other glaciers and icefields around the province that are areas of concern include Lloyd George Icefield west of Fort Nelson , Castle Creek Glacier near McBride @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ in the Columbia River Basin . @@126836741 <h> How do wildfires affect our health and what can we do ? <p> In the summer of 2023 , my wife and I spent a week vacationing with our son and his family at Shuswap Lake in the BC interior . It was mid-July and many wildfires were burning out of control across Canada . <p> In the summer of 2023 , my wife and I spent a week vacationing with our son and his family at Shuswap Lake in the BC interior . It was mid-July and many wildfires were burning out of control across Canada . In fact , 2023 became a record breaking " year of fire " in which nearly a quarter of a million people were forced to flee their homes . <p> While we were there , the Shuswap area was spared and we were able to enjoy the area 's spectacular beauty . While hiking through the forest I noticed that the forest floor was covered with a lot of fallen timber and decaying plant material . It crossed my mind that should there be a fire , it would likely be @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ " - all of it exceptionally " dry " . ( Western North America was in the grips of prolonged drought and heat , propelled by climate change . ) <p> Climate change is driven by our addiction to fossil fuels as an energy source . The result is ever-increasing carbon dioxide ( CO2 ) emissions to the atmosphere and wildfires increase those emissions . <p> Unfortunately , not long after we returned to Ontario , a massive wildfire swept through the Shuswap area causing widespread destruction . <h> Health Impacts of Breathing Wildfire Smoke <p> Wildfires and other climate related disasters are increasingly threatening communities leading to rising levels of anxiety , depression and PTSD ( Post Traumatic Stress Disorder ) . Some people become so traumatized that they are unwilling to return to their community . <p> The fear and uncertainty brought on by climate change is fueling a pandemic of declining mental health in youth as they struggle with how their futures may look . Even those who live far from the wildfires but who experience smoke-laden skies and reduced air quality report an increase in emotional @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ mental health decline , health experts warn of a number of impacts to our physical health . Wildfire smoke contains a large number of toxic chemical pollutants and " fine " ( 2.5 microns or less ) particulate matter that can penetrate deep into the lungs , enter the blood stream and lodge in blood vessels and organs . Researchers have found that smokers , people with hypertension , those with chronic diseases such as heart disease or diabetes , the elderly and the very young are at greatest risk from breathing fine particulate matter . Children 's lungs are still developing in the first 5 years of life and research has shown that wildfire smoke is 10 times more harmful to these children . <p> Additionally , fine particulate pollutants can cross the placenta during pregnancy impacting the developing brain , lungs and liver of the foetus . Health experts also warn that exposure to extreme heat and air pollution during pregnancy increases the risk of miscarriage , preterm delivery and stillbirth . <p> Fine particulates can cross the blood-brain barrier to affect brain function and may lower IQ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ risk of developing autism and other neurobehavioural conditions . <p> The bottom line is that air pollution is a leading cause of illness and death globally , killing millions of people every year . Wildfire smoke is one of the most hazardous forms of air pollution due to its " cocktail " of toxic chemicals and fine particulates . Reducing air pollution will protect the public 's health and save many lives . <h> What you can do to protect you and your family from wildfire smoke <p> There are ways to minimize the negative health impacts from wildfire smoke . Keep windows and doors shut tight and install a high efficiency furnace filter ( minimum MERV 11 ) to improve indoor air quality . A good quality air cleaner with charcoal and HEPA filters in your living spaces will add additional protection . A HEPA filter will trap even the smallest particulates and the charcoal will help to absorb toxic chemical gasses which are plentiful in wildfire smoke . <p> Monitor the air quality index where you live and , if possible , avoid going outdoors when air pollution @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ too . If you venture outdoors , avoid strenuous exercise and wear an N95 mask which fits tightly to your face . While not offering much , if any protection against toxic chemicals an N95 ( or equivalent ) mask will reduce your exposure to fine particulate matter . <p> Outdoor workers have the challenge of being exposed to polluted air for prolonged periods . Wearing a respirator , or at a minimum an N95 mask while working outdoors may not always be feasible but they should be available if needed . If workers also experience a summer heat wave their health is also threatened . Extreme heat is climate change 's greatest killer . <h> Choosing our future course to better health and prosperity <p> In North America , wildfire season has become an all-year risk . What we call " fire season " now arrives sooner and lasts longer . Driven by record setting global temperatures and prolonged periods of drought in many areas , numerous wildfires occurred during last year 's fall and winter months in New Jersey , Connecticut , Oklahoma , and most dramatically California @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ January wildfires . <p> In Canada , the majority of out-of-control wildfires have occurred in our northern boreal forests but as climate change continues to accelerate , there is growing concern that lower latitude communities will also be at increased risk . A wildfire as devastating as the one that destroyed parts of Los Angeles in January could also happen to other communities including some major Canadian cities . <p> Meanwhile , Premier Doug Ford has cut $42 million from wildfire response resources and there is a critical shortage of wildland firefighters . There is also a shortage of waterbombers . @@126837041 <h> Watch ? Warning ? How we communicate severe weather in Canada <p> Tornado season has arrived for parts of Canada . Here 's a guide to how severe weather is communicated to the public . <p> With the approach of summer , forecasters will be on the lookout for more outbreaks of severe weather , and when extreme weather looms in Canada , there is a progression of statements , watches and warnings issued to inform and protect the public . <p> Here is a guide to those alerts . <h> Weather of concern <p> When active weather is expected or occurring , but there 's no current indication that conditions will be severe or extreme , Environment Canada issues a Special Weather Statement . <p> This is a text statement , giving forecasters a chance to explain unusual conditions or weather of concern that a region may soon experience - heavy rainfall , thunderstorms , strong winds , and/or high humidex values . <p> This special weather statement was issued in southwestern Ontario , on June 20 , 2018 , due to the potential for hot and humid @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ poor air quality . Credit : ECCC <p> Essentially , any conditions that would certainly affect someone 's day , but are not expected to develop to the point where they would qualify as severe weather . <p> As the name implies , a watch means that forecasters are watching for severe weather conditions to develop . <p> When a watch is active , the public need not take any specific actions in response , but they should at least stay aware of the situation , and they should be prepared to take action if severe weather conditions develop . <h> Imminent or occurring <p> When conditions advance past simply having the potential for severe weather , and severe weather is actually developing or occurring , forecasters issue a Warning . <p> Exactly when a warning is issued usually depends on what kind of weather is expected . <p> For severe thunderstorms and tornadoes , the ideal goal is to follow a specific progression , of course . First a watch is issued , and this is followed by upgrading those watches to warnings as the storms or tornadoes develop @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ effect for much of the day , and then it is replaced by a severe thunderstorm warning as the storms pop up on radar . <p> Watches ( yellow ) and warnings ( red ) are indicated across southern Saskatchewan on this sample Public Weather Alerts Map from Environment and Climate Change Canada . At this time , severe thunderstorms would have been tracking across those regions in red . Regions under the watches , to the east , could have had potentially severe storms at that time , or they may have been under watch due to the potential for the severe storms to persist into those regions . Credit : ECCC <p> Tornado watches and warnings are a somewhat special case . Tornado watches can be issued , instead of severe thunderstorm watches , in the case where weather conditions specifically indicate the potential for the development of storms capable of producing tornadoes . After that , they would simply be upgraded to warnings if the tornadic storms developed . <p> Content continues below <p> It can happen , though , that tornado watches and warnings are issued @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ severe thunderstorms is tracking across a region . Specific storms in the line could be identified as potentially tornadic , prompting a watch , or they could suddenly develop rotation , causing forecasters to immediately issue a tornado warning for those in the storm 's path . <p> Watches and warnings issued throughout southern Ontario could include a mix of alerts for severe thunderstorms and tornadoes . Credit : ECCC <p> Since there are cases when severe conditions can pop up with little notice , however , it is also possible for a warning to be issued spontaneously . <p> Although it is fairly rare , we can see this when non-severe thunderstorms suddenly encounter conditions , which were not clearly evident beforehand , that cause them to intensify and even develop rotation . In this case , forecasters would immediately issue a severe thunderstorm warning , or possibly even a tornado warning . <h> How severe is ' severe ' ? <p> What does it take for a watch or warning to be issued for severe weather ? <p> Content continues below <p> Heavy Rainfall Warning <p> The forecast @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ more , expected to fall within one hour ( 25 mm for coastal provinces and territories , 15 mm for the dry B.C. interior ) . <p> These rainfall amounts are sufficient to cause ponding on roads , overland flooding as rainfall amounts exceed the ground 's ability to absorb the water , and even flooding risks along swollen streams and rivers . <p> Severe Thunderstorm Watch <p> Conditions are favourable for a thunderstorm to develop , with the potential to produce one or more of the following : <p> Wind gusts of at least 90 km/h <p> Hail of at least two centimetres in size <p> Heavy rainfall , as above <p> In addition to the ponding and flooding concerns noted above , hail and wind from these storms can cause significant damage to property and pose a potential risk of injury . <p> Severe Thunderstorm Warning <p> A storm with one or more of the above Watch criteria is imminent , or has actually been seen on radar and/or satellite imagery , or reported by a reliable weather spotter . <p> Tornado Watch <p> Weather conditions - temperature @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ are favourable for the development of severe thunderstorms that could produce one or more tornadoes . Thunderstorms or severe thunderstorms may or may not be actually occurring for a tornado watch to be issued . <p> Content continues below <p> Tornado Warning <p> A tornado has been reported ; or when there is evidence that tornado formation is imminent , based on Doppler radar scans or reports from a reliable spotter . <p> It is important to note that , since radar does not typically see activity below the base of a storm , it is possible for a storm to show rotation on radar , and yet have no tornado affecting the ground , at that time . <p> In this case , to protect the public , the imminent threat is enough . Even if a tornado does not actually develop from the storm 's rotation , the potential danger to anyone in the storm 's path provides ample justification for ECCC forecasters to issue a tornado warning .

@@126840995 <h> Why the Scopes ' Monkey Trial ' still matters , 100 years later <p> Clarence Darrow is shown here leaning on a table in July , 1925 , during the Scopes evolution trial in which he defended John Thomas Scopes , a teacher who taught Darwinism in a public school.The Associated Press <p> The room is inviting , comfortable but not sleepy , the abode of a curious mind . Bookcases and collection drawers line the walls . Specimen jars catch the light that streams in from the larger laboratory outside -- a sprawling , verdant garden in the heart of the English countryside . <p> Here at Down house , his family residence , Charles Darwin once sat with a writing board across his lap , carefully constructing an argument that would forever transform our understanding of the living world , and our own place in it . <p> Published in 1859 , On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection elegantly expresses how variation among individuals with inherited traits in a competition for survival can lead , over time , to " endless forms , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ an idea born out of Darwin 's observations of the astonishing wildlife he encountered as a young man in the Gal ? pagos Islands and elsewhere during a five-year voyage aboard the HMS Beagle . But it took two decades more to gestate in this quiet pocket of Victorian-era privilege . Even today , the idyllic settingstands in contrast to the book 's turbulent reception . <p> Darwin 's study at Down House where " On the Origin of Species " was written.Ivan Semeniuk/The Globe and Mail <p> While Darwin was not alone in the conclusions he reached , his formulation of the theory of evolution was uniquely comprehensive and accessible . This made its implications inescapable : All organisms are related through distant ancestors that passed on useful adaptations to succeeding generations . By extension , humans are not products of a separate , divine creation , but one of innumerable branches on an ever-diverging tree of life . <p> Satirists of the day were quick to seize on how ridiculous it all seemed . " Am I a man and a brother ? " reads the caption under @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ in May , 1861 . But for many , the sheer coherence of Origin made it too powerful to ignore . <p> " Darwin had voluminous evidence on his side , " write Alexander and Harold Gouzoules in the opening chapter oftheir new book , The Hundred Years ' Trial . When packaged in Darwin 's clear , measured prose , the theory of evolution arrived " with such an abrupt impact as to be perceived as a threat to traditional hierarchies and ideas . " <p> Now a tourist site , Darwin 's home and workplace marks the birthplace of a revolution , but the battles that followed would take place in other settings . <p> In the Gouzoulesesaccount , the father and son writing team begin with Darwin 's theory but thenmove briskly toward the explosive reactions it engendered . The main part of the book is concerned with the proceedings that unfolded in a Tennessee courtroom starting 100 years ago -- July 10 , 1925 -- when a high-school teacher named John Scopes was tried for presenting the concept of human evolution in the classroom . <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ " lasted 11 days , returning a guilty verdict with a $100 fine that was later overturned on a technicality . But the trial 's anticlimactic outcome belies its undiminished relevance a century later . <p> From the outset , the authors write , their aim was not to cast the Scopes trial as a controversy long concluded . Rather , it is a live wire that leads directly to political and cultural conflicts playing out in the U.S. today and reverberating around the globe . <p> " I do n't think it 's out of the question that what was presumably settled for decades and decades " is now up for debate , said Harold Gouzoules ( the elder of the two ) in an interview . " I think that door is being opened again . " <p> High school biology teacher John T. Scopes , seen in this July , 1925 file photo , was tried for teaching human evolution.The Associated Press <p> That was evident in 2022 , when the U.S. Supreme Court set aside the Lemon test , the byproduct of a 50-year-old ruling used @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ church and state . Adding fuel to a smouldering judicial fire , the newly re-elected Donald Trump this year issued an executive order requiring his administration to eradicate " anti-Christian bias . " <p> More broadly , the authors note , the case of Scopes v. Tennessee is a " tailor-made analogy " for more recent conflicts over issues that hinge on the role of science in public policy making , including climate change and vaccination . And in the absence of a clear mechanism that explained the rules of heredity , it was hard to understand why adaptive traits were not simply diluted out of existence by a population 's prevailing characteristics . <p> What was missing then @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ evolution works because DNA acts as both a library that can preserve useful traits and a roulette wheel that generates endless new combinations . <p> Meanwhile , an incomplete understanding of Darwin 's theory frequently turned it into a justification for racial inequality and exploitation of the poor . Pollen allergies are so common they feel like a seasonal norm ; however , the impact is anything but small . Each year , hay fever leads to the loss of an estimated 100 million school and workdays . Rates of hay fever have been rising for decades , and the pace of this increase ca n't be pinned on genetics alone . Hygiene , antibiotics , diet , air pollution and climate change are all likely contributors . <p> One treatment option is allergen-specific immunotherapy ( AIT ) , where patients are slowly desensitized to the allergen through repeated exposure over years . It does n't work for everyone , and the time and effort involved limit its use . <p> Recently , monoclonal antibody treatments have emerged as an alternative . These treatments typically involve injections and aim to stop allergic reactions by blocking either the allergen or the allergic response itself . However , they do n't target the site where most allergies start -- the nose . <p> Mugwort pollen is one of the main triggers of hay fever in Central Asia and large parts @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the idea of delivering an allergen-specific antibody straight into the nose . <h> Nasal antibody treatment reduced hay fever symptoms <p> To develop the treatment , the team first immunized mice with mugwort pollen extract , triggering the mice to produce antibodies against the allergen . They then harvested spleen cells and fused them with cancer cells to create hybridomas -- cell lines that could produce monoclonal antibodies indefinitely . <p> Of the five hybridomas created , one stood out : clone XA19 . It showed a strong ability to block IgE , the antibody that triggers allergic reactions , from binding to the mugwort allergen Art v 1 in both human and mouse samples . <p> The researchers then tested XA19 in a mouse model of hay fever and asthma . Mice were sensitized to mugwort pollen to mimic allergic responses . Some of the mice were treated with intranasal XA19 just before each of the three allergen exposures . The researchers compared these with a placebo group and a group that had n't been sensitized . <p> Treated mice showed fewer signs of allergy : less nose rubbing @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ samples from the nose and lungs showed less inflammation and levels of IL-4 and IL-5 , cytokines involved in allergy and asthma , were lower . <p> " Our method acts immediately and locally at the lining of the nose , by neutralizing the allergen on contact . How many are you ready to try ? <h> Fear is fueling democratic decline but you can contribute to changing the course <h> Key points <p> Increase in negative emotions in the last two decades predicted increases in populism undermining democracy <p> We need to break the cycle of negative social media content , negative emotions and populism <p> You can make a difference by using fear as a compass , fostering shared humanity and taking constructive action <p> Majority of people in the USA across the political spectrum who were surveyed in July 2025 , 76% on average , agreed that democracy in their country is under serious threat . This is not just an abstract statistic , the strength of democracy impacts on many aspects of people 's lives across the globe - from what information they are allowed to access through their trust in the justice system to how they are educated @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ strong democracies ( and this does not include only rich democratic countries ) are more likely to be happy . <p> What is responsible for this coupling between negative emotions and populism ? First , during the past two decades negative feelings towards political opponents were more effective in mobilising political participation than before . Accordingly , politicians have been increasingly resorting to tactics inciting negative emotions towards their opponents to attract followers . Second , alongside these political developments the use of social media increased exponentially . Negative content , including polarised political views , is reposted on these platforms more , thus encouraging sharing of negative opinions . <p> As a result , we are currently stuck in a vicious cycle of population-wide negative emotions feeding populism and thus undermining democracy enabled by social media promoting polarised political views and fueling further worry and fear . This cycle impacts on our collective ability to tackle current global crises . For example , research shows that strong democracies are better able to faciliated transitions to new economic and societal models needed for mitigating the effects of climate change . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ At an individual level , fear is a natural acute evolutionary response we have to a threat , and therefore it activates the stress response . Fear narrows our attention and makes us ready to fight , flee or freeze in the face of danger , increasing our chances of survival . The problem is that the fear we are experiencing in the context of democratic decline is not short-lived ; we ca n't easily run away from the danger . <p> Such persistent fear can turn into chronic anxiety and further diminish our individual and collective abilities to change the course of democratic decline . This is because fear and anxiety increase the release of stresshormones , particularly cortisol , which are neurotoxic . These hormones can damage brain areas underpinning our working memory , decision making and learning - the prefrontal cortex and the hippocampus . <p> Such changes in the brain make it in turn harder for us to engage with complex information when solutions to problems are not apparent - for example , when we are trying to figure out possible causes of economic downturn . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ conspiracies - often blaming some groups or institutions for negative societal developments - because they provide simple solutions . They give us a false sense of security - having any explanation , albeit implausible , can feel better than the fear arising from not having a straightforward explanation at hand . <p> Scaled up , this is how fear and anxiety - incited by politicians for political gain and enabled by social media - impact our ability to consider information carefully , connect with others and ultimately find solutions to societal problems affecting our lives . In this way , fear propels the cycle connecting negative emotions and democratic decline in perpetuity . Breaking this cycle should be our individual and collective priority , but how ? <h> Step 1 : Use fear as a compass <p> As the first step , we need to reduce the negative impacts of fear on our ability to make decisions and solve problems . This means applying self-care strategies to mitigate the impacts of fear and anxiety on our mind and brain . To start with , we can simply acknowledge emotions that @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ this in itself can reduce the intensity of negative emotions . In addition , making time for activities in our daily life that help us relax and recharge - be they socialising with others , exercise or hobbies - can make a lot of difference to our mental health and wellbeing . <p> Mindfulness is a common approach to reducing stress and anxiety that can be helpful too . This can take on many different forms . For instance , we can anchor our attention on sensory experiences in the present moment in an accepting and nonjudgmental way , such as listening to sounds in our environment without elaboration . Another option might be going on a mindful walk or taking a few mindful breaths with longer outbreaths - this increases activity in the parasympathetic nervous system linked to resting and digesting and reduces the fight/flight/freeze response . <p> Bringing the levels of fear and anxiety down may then enable us to start using fear as a compass - as a navigation system that shows us what matters to us . In this way , fear can alert us to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ give direction to our efforts . So the goal of the first step is not to eliminate fear , but to use it skillfully to motivate , discern and guide our actions in the next two steps . However , without taking this first step , fear is more likely to lead to overwhelm , fruitless engagement with conspiracies online or ' paralysis ' where we feel hopeless and unable to take effective action . <h> Step 2 : Do n't lose your humanity <p> The use of fear-based strategies by politicians has consequences for how we view others . After inciting fear in their followers , politicians often tend to provide a solution to the fear by pointing to something or someone to blame - these can be democratic institutions , or some groups of people based on their profession , ethnic origin , colour of skin , education level etc . This makes the cause of the fear concrete , and therefore easier to address and cope with . <p> Such a strategy also makes it more likely for people to accept politically-driven enforcement action that they would @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ others . This is how political polarisation can translate into dehumanisation - perceiving those that are supposedly to blame for some societal issues as less than human . <p> Dehumanisation bypasses our biological tendencies of empathy and caring for others that helped humans survive . For example , neuroscience research shows that areas of the brain that are activated when we are in pain closely overlap with those brain areas that become active when we are witnessing others ' pain . Dehumanisation aims to dampen this evolutionary survival mechanism and thus enable violence against others without much resistance . <p> Yet , research on those who do resist dehumanisation of others under the conditions of authoritarianism or dictatorship shows that they have a strong sense of shared humanity . They are people who show more empathy towards others , are more compassionate , caring and forgiving . They also have strong moral values and believe that justice , liberty and equality should apply to everyone . This is why we need to foster our shared humanity and use it to guide us towards effective solutions in order to strengthen democracy @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , now that you are equipped with the motivation to contribute to a positive change using fear as a compass coupled with shared humanity , you might be ready to take action to support democracy . Here it is important to dedicate energy to efforts that can make a real-world difference . So you may want to start by exploring ways you can use your professional knowledge and skills in this process . <p> This may initially involve educating yourself about pillars of democracy - including independent journalism , strong court system , science-based decision making and evidence-based education . Understanding and working with your fear skillfully is the key to being able to discern truth , foster trust and shared humanity , and take constructive action to strengthen democracy . Perhaps such a mindset and resulting action , taken at individual and collective levels , is the best tool we have at our disposal to change the direction of democratic decline with its wide-reaching consequences for our way of life , wellbeing and ability to tackle current intertwined crises . <p> Life never gets easier . Flowers are nice , of course , but focusing on beauty can seem like a frill amid the crises of our times , from war to a warming planet . <p> Show attendees take a peak at the toilet in the Garden of the Future.ADRIAN DENNIS/AFP/Getty Images <p> But if a thing of beauty is a joy forever -- as Keats wrote in his poem Endymion -- the stunning Chelsea Flower Show is proof that beauty can be of the moment and practical , too , changing with our evolving needs and concerns . Each garden , exhibit or plant at Chelsea implements important environmental functions with a new , gorgeous naturalism that delivers the powerful message at the heart of the show : even with just a container or two , we all have the ability to make incremental , much-needed contributions to help mitigate the harmful effects of climate change . That idea has clearly taken root in Britain -- that beauty is n't necessarily a frill or a distraction , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ be allowed to bloom here in Canada , too . <p> Many of our current beliefs and attitudes about beauty as an indulgence are shaped by debates from the beginnings of Western aesthetics in the 18th century . The rise of the arts in the West at that time was accompanied by the birth of philosophical aesthetics , which aimed to explain the nature and experience of beautiful art . Yet focusing on the arts when we think about beauty has had unfortunate consequences . <p> Unlike cups or buildings or bridges , paintings or sculptures or pieces of music do n't have practical functions -- and so , over time , we in the West came to think of the functional and the beautiful as being distinct . It seemed that things could carry out their functions just as well without being beautiful , and so , beauty came to be viewed as little more than a bonus . <p> It is undeniable that beauty is a powerful draw ; no one doubts its seductive power . But often , we assume that in hard circumstances -- when there @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ world feels like it 's on fire -- we can set beauty aside to carry on with what really needs to get done . Though this view underlies many of our ordinary attitudes toward beauty , we should reconsider it . After all , there is no question that beauty plays an integral role in the ways people live . <p> A few thinkers have tried to convince us of this . For example , the late 19th-century designer and social activist William Morris used beautiful design to counter the tide of mass production that he believed denuded everyday life of beauty . In the early 20th century , American philosopher John Dewey argued that ordinary perception is fulfilled -- taken to its full potential -- in aesthetic experiences that can be prompted by ordinary things in everyday life . <p> By the late 20th century , several contemporary philosophers followed Dewey to argue that not only the arts , but also the environment and the commonplace , can be repositories of beauty or aesthetic value . <p> I believe this is important , because beauty is not simply a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ value that shapes and enriches human life . <p> A visitor stops to look through a magnifying glass on the ' This Humid House ' installation by Tabula Rosa.Leon Neal/Getty Images <p> Our day-to-day lives can hold aesthetic value in many different ways : in ordinary objects or clothing , in everyday rituals or events , in our actions in sports or dance . And now , technology has made the arts and their aesthetic features a large part of everyday life : We plug ourselves into music , binge hours of narrative arts and enjoy the ubiquity of images vying for our attention at all times . There is no question that our aesthetic experiences -- and experiences of beauty , if we are lucky -- and the things they engage with are an enormous part of human life . <p> This brings us back to gardens , which have united beauty with function as a core part of human life since ancient times . @@126923425 <p> July 14 , 2000 will always be remembered as one of the darkest days in the history of central Alberta . <p> It may even be a bit surreal to realize that this Monday is the Pine Lake tornado 's 25th anniversary . <p> Twelve people died that day , and hundreds sustained injuries , many of them severe . The tornado ranks as the second deadliest in Alberta history , and the fourth worst in Canadian history after 1894 in Huron , Ontario , 1987 in Edmonton , and 1946 in Windsor , Ontario . <p> As encapsulated in a 2020 article by former rdnewsNOW news director Troy Gillard : <p> The tornado , categorized as an F3 with wind speeds up to 300 km/h and ranging from 800 metres to 1.5 kilometres wide , carved a 15-kilometre path of destruction . <p> The storm started developing around 4 p.m. along the Rocky Mountain foothills , and at 6:18 p.m. , Environment Canada issued a severe thunderstorm warning . I thought , ' Oh boy , they 're going to get rained on really good , ' " says Claggett , who was working as a journalist in Red Deer at the time . <p> ( Red Deer Archives ) <p> Ten years after the tornado , Claggett interviewed the first paramedic and ambulance driver to arrive on scene at Green Acres . <p> " He stopped his ambulance and got on the microphone and said , ' We 're going to need way @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ then went down and started working , " Claggett recalls , likening it , in principle , to a journalist 's work when tough news stories such as this occur . <p> " You see the situation , you assess , and then you do what you 're supposed to do , which is get information out . " <p> Claggett was working as a news director in Wetaskiwin on July 31 , 1987 when the Black Friday tornado killed 27 people in Edmonton . <p> Pine Lake brought him back to that experience , which he drew upon in reporting on it , including when he visited the campsite a few days after . <p> " There are so many situations you do n't expect to come across your desk , and when they do , you just handle it , " he shares . <p> " You have to vacate your personal feelings and focus on the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , and get it out as quickly and as accurately as possible . @@126923561 <p> Life never gets easier . Fortunately , psychology is keeping up , uncovering new ways to maintain mental and physical health , and positivity and confidence , through manageable daily habits like these . How many are you ready to try ? <h> Navigating doomsday fears in a changing world . <h> Key points <p> Coping with existential dread and the collective anxiety sometimes requires trying new things . <p> Doomsday fears are inspired by cognitive distortions where we automatically assume the worst-case scenario . <p> Concentrating on what you have control over gives you a sense of purpose amid the darkness . <p> Racing thoughts , tension in your muscles , fear in the pit of your stomach , and the alarming sense that disaster is imminent are the trademarks of our modern-day world-weariness . Whether it 's work , relationships , a volatile economy , wars overseas , political divisiveness , climate change , technology-induced anxiety -- or a combination of all -- these have added to the collective worry that causes us to conjure up doomsday scenarios of the future . However , while recognizing potential @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , getting caught in a cycle of spiraling fear can be harmful to our well-being . <p> Hence , coping with existential dread and the collective anxiety sometimes requires altering the narrative and trying new things . The following tips are merely a sampling of the many strategies we can use when we are worried about future change . How do we traverse the rugged terrain of " what if " thinking and retrieve our peace of mind ? <h> Get " Philosophical " <p> Getting " philosophical " means using this time as an opportunity to develop a different relationship with your worry and fear . There are benefits of walking toward the pain as opposed to walking away from it . The relatively recent concept of allostasis ( stability through change ) refers to the mind 's way of achieving emotional steadiness through adaptive responses to adversity , not by circumventing it . In other words , stop resisting change . <p> So instead of running from the feelings and making them worse , try to embrace them in a way that will build emotional resilience instead of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ a distressing one . When negative feelings are processed properly , exposure to them actually can make us wiser over time . But in the end , emotional resilience is not about grit ; it 's about learning to convert adversity into thriving . <h> Accept Your Feelings <p> This is a clich ? , of course , but acceptance of how you are feeling ( even if you are distressed ) might be a good place to start . You are scared because the human mind is designed to prioritize danger . It 's how we have stayed alive for thousands of years . Hence , you will feel better if you focus less on the context ( the details of whatever you 're afraid of ) and more on reducing the activated feelings that are getting generated . <p> The trick is to treat your symptoms , not try to resist change or talk yourself out of your fearful thoughts . It 's OK to be scared , and it 's OK to be worried . Hence , acceptance is your inflection point . It 's your existential @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , " What the future holds for you depends on your state of consciousness now . " <h> Examine the Evidence <p> A good technique for challenging fearful thinking is to separate yourself from the emotional involvement with your negative thoughts . If you are confronted by an episode of anxiety , examine the evidence by looking deeply into the statements you are telling yourself . Ask : Is this an opinion or an absolute fact ? Is it interpretation or reality ? <p> Typically , doomsday fears are inspired by cognitive distortions where we automatically assume the worst-case scenario . By carefully examining the likelihood of your fears becoming a reality , you gradually debunk them and loosen the grip they have on you . Otherwise , they will continue to be experienced as rock-bottom data or become fearful projections and predictions that are unfounded . <h> This Too Shall Pass ( Seriously , It Will ) <p> It 's another overused chestnut , but it 's good to remember that adversity and tough times are temporary setbacks and are not indicative of the rest of our lives . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , and even tragedy give us strength in many ways and force us to develop adaptive tools for the future . They fortify our coping mechanisms and help us build distress tolerance skills . <p> Remember , if stress were not useful to the human organism , evolution would have eliminated it a long time ago . It exists for a reason . It 's an adaptive function that is here to stay . <h> Be a Good Historian <p> Think back on times in your life when you have faced adversity : loss of job , financial hardship , illness , a bad breakup , death in the family , natural disaster . Now , remember how you got through it ( I often ask my therapy clients to make a list ) . Remember how difficult it was for you . Remember how depressed and scared you were at the time . Then , remember how good it felt after you survived it . Rely on your past experiences of triumph to draw strength in this experience today . Learn to be a mindful historian . You 're @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ S ? ren Kierkegaard , " Life must be understood backwards ; but ... it must be lived forwards . " <h> Maintain Structure <p> Stay busy and focused . Just as with the pandemic of 2020 and any other type of catastrophic event , resist the temptation to become inconsistent with your daily routines , your rituals , and your responsibilities . Do n't let the dejection affect your motivation to the point of changing the rhythms of your life . Do n't allow yourself to become resigned to the fear and think , " what 's the point ? " Remain consistent and go about life as it was before . We are creatures of habit . If you lose your structure and consistency , your distress could increase . <p> Remember , there is even psychological value in regularly performing commonplace duties , such as throwing out the trash , tidying up your room , flossing your teeth , and helping your kids do their homework . <h> Focus on What You Have Control Over <p> To reduce the fear and powerlessness that is affecting you , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ you . You will also feel more confident and will learn to trust yourself better . In other words , ground yourself in the present by zeroing in on yourself , your family , your job , personal projects , and chores around the house . Concentrating on what you have control over gives you a sense of agency ; it gives you a sense of purpose amid the darkness . <h> Be Careful With " What If " Thinking <p> Be careful with all of the catastrophic outcomes you are creating in your head about how change might negatively affect you . It 's important to care about important issues , but it 's irrational to toy with futuristic , fear-scaping thinking . <p> We do n't know what 's going to happen , and sometimes that 's OK . For now , stay realistic and remember that future-based thinking is only the play of thought ; it 's not real . Stop fictionalizing tomorrow with apocalyptic scenarios . It will make you feel better . <p> Finally , in our rapidly changing world , doomsday fears will always @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ our minds for longer than we want , but they do n't have to control us . We can find a healthy balance of acknowledging them without needing to succumb to them . <p> Life never gets easier . Fortunately , psychology is keeping up , uncovering new ways to maintain mental and physical health , and positivity and confidence , through manageable daily habits like these . How many are you ready to try ?

@@126944403 <h> Hey old bird : A 33-year-old puffin on New Brunswick island going strong , with a chick <p> A 33-year-old puffin , seen in this handout photo , was found on Machias Seal Island , N.B. , by University of New Brunswick researchers in July 2025 . THE CANADIAN PRESS/Handout - Daniel Oliker , UNB ( Mandatory Credit ) <p> FREDERICTON -- Daniel Oliker held a 33-year-old puffin from Machias Seal Island in his hands and was in awe about how it was a decade older than him . It felt like he was holding a world of knowledge and history in that puff ball of black and white feathers . <p> The University of New Brunswick graduate student , researching Atlantic puffin ecology , found a bird with a plastic band dating back to 1992 . It showed the tuxedo bird to be a wise and worldly 33 . And it had a chick . <p> Machias Seal Island is a flat , treeless sanctuary for seabirds located about 19 kilometres southwest of New Brunswick 's Grand Manan Island at the mouth @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ breeding pairs of puffins . <p> Oliker said last week his fellow researcher spotted one of the tuxedo birds on the island with a faded , green-and-white plastic band , and marked the area where it was seen . Those bands were used by Canada Wildlife Services starting in the 1970s until around 1995 , when they started being replaced with metal ones . <p> Around midnight Oliker and a couple of researchers went to search the burrows -- nests where puffins rest at night after a day at sea -- looking for the old bird . <p> After searching a few burrows , he said he found the right bird by feeling the bands on their legs . A few had metal bands . <p> " Then I felt one that felt a little bit different , and it was in the right location that we marked so I pulled it out and it was the right guy , " he said in an interview from the island . <p> The old bird was curious and did n't put up much of a fight when it was pulled out @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ metal one , giving the puffin its new number : JG18 . But they do n't yet know its gender . <p> That he was holding one of the oldest birds , Oliker said , was " very exciting " and " truly amazing . " Most puffins in the wild live up to their mid-20s . <p> " Just to think of how many years he spent out on the open ocean . How deep he 's dived before . " <p> The chick was a " decent size , " which was pleasantly surprising because puffins are struggling this year from a seeming lack of food , he said . " It 's very likely , because he 's been alive for so long , that he knows which spots might be better for fish . " <p> Puffins start reproducing around four or five so JG18 has probably had more than 25 chicks in its lifetime even if all did n't survive , Oliker said . <p> Nick Lund , a network manager for U.S. wildlife conservation organization Maine Audubon , said one of the biggest threats facing Atlantic puffins in the Gulf of Maine is climate change . <p> " The Gulf of Maine is the southernmost breeding area for puffins in the Atlantic , but the water is warming very quickly , " he noted . <p> " New fish species are moving in to the warming waters , and other fish species -- those traditionally eaten by puffins -- are moving out . @@126954304 <h> How ideology can trump self-interest <p> U.S. President Donald Trump 's spending and tax bill phases out the clean-energy subsidies introduced during former president Joe Biden 's administration three years ago.Michael Conroy/The Associated Press <p> Among the disasters of U.S. President Donald Trump 's " One Big Beautiful Bill , " one is particularly stinging for political economists : it radically phases out the clean-energy subsidies introduced during former president Joe Biden 's administration three years ago . <p> These subsidies were considered by many as immune to a change of presidents , because they created new jobs and profit opportunities for firms in traditionally Republican-voting " red " states . As allergic as the Trump-controlled Republican Party is to green policies , the conventional wisdom was that it would not dare take away these benefits . <p> So where did the conventional wisdom go wrong ? Scholars who study how political decisions are made tend to focus on economic costs and benefits . They reason that legislation that creates material gains for organized , well-connected groups at the expense of diffuse losses to the rest of society are @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Trump 's bill are indeed well explained by this perspective : in particular , it engineers a dramatic transfer of income to the wealthy at the expense of the poor . <p> By the same token , legislation that creates concentrated losses for powerful economic interests is unlikely to make much headway . This explains , for example , why raising the price of carbon , a requirement for fighting climate change but a big hit to fossil-fuel interests , has been a politically toxic non-starter in the U.S. <p> Mr. Biden 's green-energy program , the Inflation Reduction Act ( IRA ) , was designed to overcome this political obstacle . Instead of wielding a stick -- carbon taxation -- it offered carrots in the form of subsidies for solar , wind , and other renewables . The idea was that in time , as people benefitted from the subsidies and the green lobbies strengthened , perhaps even a direct push against fossil fuels would become politically feasible . <p> These hopes have been shattered . The green lobbies did try to soften the bill 's anti-IRA provisions , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and solar tax credits until mid-2026 . But while the IRA has not been repealed in full , the Democrats ' anticipated green transition now lies in tatters . <p> Those who subscribe to the materialist version of political economy will find ways to rationalize the reversal . The regressive tax cuts for the rich required that revenues be found elsewhere , so perhaps a less influential interest group was sacrificed for a more powerful one . Or maybe three years were not enough for IRA subsidies to create a strong enough lobby in their favour . <p> Ultimately , though , these excuses ring false . We need to accept that ideology sometimes trumps material interests . There can be little doubt that many Republican lawmakers voted against their constituents ' economic interests -- some because they feared reprisals from Mr. Trump , others because they truly are climate skeptics and , like the President , oppose anything that smacks of green activism . Regardless , ideas about what is important and how the world works prevailed over economic lobbies or vested interests . <p> There is a broader @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ politics in gaining traction for a party 's agenda . The ability to shape worldviews and ideologies -- of elites as well as ordinary voters -- is a powerful weapon . Those who have it can persuade people to make choices that seem to conflict with their economic interests . <p> In fact , interests themselves , economic or otherwise , are shaped by ideas . In order to figure out whether we gain or lose from a particular policy , we need to know how the policy will play out in the real world , and also what would happen in the absence of the policy . Few among us have the ability or inclination to figure it out . Ideologies offer shortcuts to such complicated decision-making processes . Some of these ideologies take the form of stories and narratives about how the world works . A right-wing politician , for example , might say " government intervention always backfires " ; others focus on increasing the salience of various types of identities -- ethnic , religious , or political . Depending on context , the message could be @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ your enemy . " <p> Importantly , the concept of " self-interest " itself relies on an implicit idea about who the " self " is : who we are , distinct from others , and what our purpose is . These ideas are not fixed in nature or at birth . An alternative tradition in political economy views interests as socially constructed rather than determined by material circumstances . Depending on whether we identify as " white male , " " working-class , " or " evangelical , " for example , we will see our interests differently . As constructivists might say , " interest is an idea . " <p> So for Mr. Trump 's opponents to succeed , they must do more than produce well-designed policies that yield material benefits for targeted groups . Whether it is in fighting climate change , promoting America 's national security , or creating good jobs , they need to win the larger battle of ideas -- particularly the ideas that shape voters ' understanding of who they are and where their interests lie . Democrats , in particular , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ recently left many ordinary Americans behind -- just like the pre-Biden economic policies that contributed to Mr. Trump 's rise .

We must treat it that way . <p> Whether it 's a construction site , a delivery route , a farm , a factory floor or a commercial kitchen , Canadian workers are sweating it out in conditions that would be considered unsafe in any other context . Heat stress is n't the new normal . It is a serious occupational hazard , just like exposure to toxic chemicals or operating heavy machinery . <p> And the risks are real -- heat stroke , dehydration , exhaustion , fainting . Heat exposure has also been linked to heart attacks , kidney damage , pregnancy complications and other chronic health conditions . In indoor workplaces that are already hot -- such as bakeries , industrial kitchens , or warehouses without ventilation -- the danger only multiplies . Many long-term care facilities and schools are decades old , poorly ventilated and lack adequate cooling . These are not just comfort issues . They are questions of dignity , safety and health . <p> Shockingly , only 30 per cent of schools in Toronto 's public system have air conditioning . Educational workers and our children are trying to teach and learn in the same oppressive heat many workers are forced to labour in . @@127016409 <h> Weather Alert <p> Take action to protect yourself and others -- extreme heat can affect everyone 's health . Determine if you or others around you are at greater risk of heat illness . Check on older adults , those living alone and other at-risk people in-person or on the phone multiple times a day . @@127020872 <h> Hotter world means less milk , study finds <p> HOT COWS -- New research suggests that climate change could put a big dent in milk production even with the use of cooling technologies . Cows in Israel produced about 10 per cent less milk after one day of +26 C conditions . KEVIN MA/St . Albert Gazette <p> Alberta farmers will get less milk from their cows in the years ahead because of global heating , even if they use the latest in cooling technologies , a new study suggests . <p> Agricultural economics professor Ayal Kimhi of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem co-authored a study July 5 in Science Advances on the effects of extreme heat events on milk production . <p> Heat-trapping pollution primarily from fossil fuels is putting Canadians at greater risk of extreme heat . St. Albert is set to experience about eight times more plus-30 C days a year than it does today by the 2060s ( about 24.3 compared to the current 3.1 ) , the city 's climate adaptation plan reports . <p> Heat affects cows , with Israel 's cows producing @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ in the cool winter , Kimhi said . He and his team sought to find out just how badly heat affects milk production and the degree to which technology can help offset its effects . <h> Hot cows <p> To do so , they took the daily milk production records of about 130,000 cows in Israel over 12 years and linked them to hourly local weather reports , and surveyed about 300 farmers about their use of cooling technologies . <p> The team found that a cow 's milk output dropped significantly on hot , humid days . Cows produced about 9.6 per cent less milk per day when the wet-bulb temperature ( a measure that accounts for both heat and humidity ) exceeded 26 C , compared to 3.7 per cent less at 22-24 C and 1.6 per cent less at 18-20 C. It took cows more than 10 days to get back to regular production levels after being exposed to a day of plus-26 C heat . <p> Cows have to spend more energy on sweating when it 's hot , which means less energy for milk production @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ hot days , cows can produce up to 10 per cent less milk . " <p> While almost everyone in Israel uses fans , sprayers , and other techniques to keep cows cool , the team found these measures did not fully offset losses caused by extreme heat . At 18-20 C , cooling systems cut losses by about half . At plus-24 C , they reduced them by about 40 per cent . Still , the team found that farmers that did install cooling systems for their cows would recover their costs in about 1.5 years . <p> The team noted extreme humid heat events had doubled in frequency worldwide in the last 40 years and were predicted to become widespread because of global heating . Without efforts to adapt , such heating could cut milk production among major producers by four per cent by 2050 . <h> Adaptation limits <p> " Climate change will have wide-ranging impacts on what we eat and drink , including that cold glass of milk , " study co-author Eyal Frank said in a media release . <p> " Our study found that @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ supply , and even the most high-tech , well-resourced farms are deploying adaptation strategies that may be an insufficient match to climate change . " <p> Kimhi said farmers could compensate for heat-related losses by raising more cows , but that would mean higher costs and more cow-related heat-trapping pollution . Farmers may have to instead pick cows that are more heat-resistant , even if they are less productive ; their study found that the most productive cows were also the most heat-sensitive . <p> Extreme heat does put a damper on milk production , said Jason Crozier of Sturgeon County 's Cheslen Dairies . He uses high ceilings , temperature-controlled windows , and " big-ass fans " to keep his cows cool , while farmers in hotter areas like Arizona use water sprayers . Farmers will likely have to get more fans and heat-resistant cows to compensate for the heat-related losses predicted in this study . <p> " At the end of the day , we just want to keep those cows happy , and when they are happy , they produce better . " <h> This has been @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ in 2006 . He writes about Sturgeon County , education , the environment , agriculture , science and aboriginal affairs . He also contributes features , photographs and video .

@@127062900 <h> Weather Alert <p> Take action to protect yourself and others -- extreme heat can affect everyone 's health . Determine if you or others around you are at greater risk of heat illness . Check on older adults , those living alone and other at-risk people in-person or on the phone multiple times a day . Watch for the early signs of heat exhaustion in yourself and others . Signs may include headache , nausea , dizziness , thirst , dark urine and intense fatigue . Stop your activity and drink water . Heat stroke is a medical emergency ! Call 9-1-1 or your emergency health provider if you , or someone around you , is showing signs of heat stroke which can include red and hot skin , dizziness , nausea , confusion and change in consciousness . While you wait for medical attention , try to cool the person by moving them to a cool place , removing extra clothing , applying cold water or ice packs around the body . Drink water often and before you feel thirsty to replace fluids . Close blinds , or @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . Turn on air conditioning , use a fan , or move to a cooler area of your living space . Plan and schedule outdoor activities during the coolest parts of the day . Limit direct exposure to the sun and heat . Wear lightweight , light-coloured , loose-fitting clothing and a wide-brimmed hat . Never leave people , especially children , or pets inside a parked vehicle . The first is by consuming uncooked or undercooked shellfish , like oysters . <p> The second method is by entering affected seawater with an open wound . And in the United States , couples surveyed reported having 58 money-related arguments per year . <p> The economic barriers to independence are particularly pronounced for those contemplating separation or divorce . Traditionally , a breakup meant one partner moving out , but now more divorced and separated couples are finding themselves cohabitating simply because they ca n't afford to live alone . <h> Postponing major life decisions <p> The cost-of-living crisis is also delaying key life milestones for young adults worldwide . Doug Ford of Ontario said much the same about his province 's order for six more bombers . <p> Six weeks later , the country is well into one of its worst wildfire seasons ever . <p> As of Thursday , the number of new fires in Canada ( 3,235 ) was higher than at the same point last year ( 3,145 ) , according to the Canadian Interagency Forest Fire Centre . More than 5.5 million hectares of forest have burned . <p> The fires get worse every summer , thanks to the heat and drought caused @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ for suppression over mitigation that has left forest floors littered with flammable material and created a denser canopy at the top where flames can spread , well , like wildfire . <p> And yet Canada 's premiers still focus on suppression while experts -- including some in their own governments -- keep telling them to put equal effort and money into ignition prevention and mitigation : in particular , prescribed burns . <p> " Suppression alone is no longer adequate to address the growing challenges from wildland fire , " the Canadian Council of Forest Ministers said in a report last year . " Wildland fire management in Canada needs to be transformed . " <p> That means creating a national regime of prescribed burns -- the deliberate setting of fires under controlled circumstances to reduce the number and intensity of forest fires , and to limit damage to property . <p> It 's a practice that Indigenous peoples in Canada and elsewhere used for millennia to manage their lands prior to the colonial era . But its use is sharply limited in Canada , mostly because politicians are scared @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ government-sanctioned burn could get out of control ( as has rarely happened ) . <p> This reticence is no longer valid in the climate change era . Australia responded to massive wildfires in 2019 by becoming a world leader in the use of prescribed burns , partly by integrating Aboriginal knowledge into its practices . <p> Tens of millions of hectares of Australian lands are now subject to prescribed burns each year , and the result has been fewer and less intense wildfires , less damage to property , massive savings on expensive suppression efforts and a net drop of carbon emissions . <p> In Canada , only a few thousand hectares of land are subject to prescribed burns each year , mostly in national parks . The country 's aversion to the practice is being traded off against severe wildfires that this year have forced 30,000 people from their homes , and which pump harmful smoke into the air Canadians breath ( an issue we will address in an upcoming editorial ) . <p> Canada has to grow up and embrace prescribed burns . To do that , it @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to respond to the now perennial forest-fire emergency , and which can also tend to the off-season task of planning and carrying out prescribed fires . <p> Australia has more than 140,000 trained volunteer forest fire fighters who manage the prescribed burns , and also respond to outbreaks during fire season . <p> Canada , meanwhile , leaves suppression to the provinces and territories , which rely on seasonal professionals to battle fires . Those firefighters are routinely overwhelmed by the scale of the fires , requiring Canada to call on other countries to send reinforcements , and to back-order more water bombers in desperation . <p> It 's becoming clear that the country with the world 's largest boreal forest is not up to the task of managing it . This failure is made more damning by the fact that Canada appears poised to increase its fossil fuel production , which could contribute to the climate-change crisis . <p> It 's going to be awfully hard to build new pipelines across a part of the country that is on fire every summer , and even harder to justify it @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and start fighting bad fire with good fire . 
@@127111132 <p> Seatless , behind in the polls , his leadership increasingly under threat , Pierre Poilievre has found the issue he thinks can revive his fortunes : immigration . No longer content with demanding tighter controls on immigration , notably in the troubled temporary foreign workers and international students programs , or even his previous demands for " severe limits on population growth , " the Conservative Leader is now calling for absolute population decline . <p> The country , he told a press conference this week , needs " very hard caps " on immigration . How hard ? Hard enough that there are " more people leaving than coming " for " the next couple years . " <p> Since immigration is and will be the sole source of population growth for the foreseeable future -- birth rates have plunged to the point that the native-born population is already in decline -- that amounts to a call for depopulation . <p> He is not alone . The conservative mediasphere is in one of its periodic frenzies over the issue . Writing in the National Post , Jamie Sarkonak @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ overpopulating " Canada and dismisses recent shifts in policy as at best a partial solution to " our crowding problem . " <p> Over at The Hub , Sabrina Maddeaux writes " Canada could n't keep up with the mass immigration targets set by Justin Trudeau 's Liberals , and recent reductions are only a first step on the path to correcting the tremendous harm done . " <p> The first thing to point out is just how radical what is being proposed really is . There has never been a year in this country 's history when it has actually shrunk in population . The slowest it has grown was in 1916 , during the First World War , when immigration , previously at an all-time peak , was all but shut down . <p> The second thing to point out is : that is already current policy . The Trudeau government , in an abrupt reversal , announced a series of drastic policy shifts last fall . The number of student permits was capped at 10 per cent below previous levels . The temporary foreign worker program was @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ residents in the population is to be reduced to 5 per cent , from about 7 per cent currently , by 2027 . How is that to be done ? By ensuring there are " more people leaving than coming . " The current target ( see chart ) is a net out-migration of non-permanent residents of over 400,000 annually , or slightly more than the 395,000 permanent residents that are to be admitted this year ( a reduction of 20 per cent from the previous target ) . <p> What 's that spell ? Absolute population decline . How long is it to last ? A couple years , as it happens . <p> You have to hand it to Mr. Poilievre . He would appear to have successfully pandered to his base 's desire for radical change -- The Hub 's editor-at-large , Sean Speer , notes approvingly " a new sharpness and urgency to his message " -- while endorsing the status quo . <p> The Liberals , for their part , continue to pose as " the party of immigration , " even as they are @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Conservative governments could only dream . <p> Not only have they sharply curtailed immigration , but refugee claimants are , as of the passage of Bill C-2 , to be denied a hearing if they have been in the country past certain arbitrary deadlines : a flatly unconstitutional provision that is almost certain to be tossed out by the Supreme Court . <p> Neither are these mere pledges of future action , that may or may not come to pass . Population growth has already slowed to a trickle : Canada added just 20,000 people to its numbers in the first quarter , the second-slowest quarterly rate of growth since 1946 , down from 63,000 in the last quarter of 2024 . <p> I hate to interrupt all this bipartisan chumminess , but is this actually a good idea ? I get that immigration was a partisan liability for the Liberals , to be dispatched , like previous Liberal pieties , the minute it became inconvenient . <p> I get , too , that the temporary foreign worker and international student programs had more or less gone wild , leaving @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ even of how many people were entering under each . <p> But is this really the time to be throwing the population engine in reverse ? Standard growth theory focuses on three main drivers : increases in labour , increases in capital , and technical improvement -- finding more productive ways to combine labour and capital . Productivity gains we know are meagre . Investment is flat on its back . The only thing we have going for us these days is labour supply . <p> Or rather , we had . But the inexorable aging of the population presents us with a decades-long dilemma , as the share of the population over the age of 65 -- and 75 , and 85 , and so on -- rises to levels our society has never seen before . Not only does that imply stratospheric levels of health care spending ( as a rule of thumb , per capita consumption of health care doubles for every decade over the age of 55 ) , but leaves us with relatively fewer people of working age to pay for it . <p> For @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ spare person-hour of labour we can possibly get our hands on . But now add some of the other major expenditures we 're facing in coming years : the billions of dollars annually for infrastructure that we 've failed to keep up , the tens of billions of dollars for defence now that we 've discovered the world is a dangerous place , the incalculable costs of slowing up , adjusting to , or compensating for climate change . <p> Why on Earth would we want to cut off the lifeline of imported labour , at this of all moments in history ? Restrictionists have an answer . Because of the terrible effects of adding all those people -- or at least all those foreign-born people : the same arguments are never mustered in favour of limiting inter-provincial migration -- to the labour market , the housing market , and the health care system . <p> The same grisly trio are always invoked . Are wages stagnant ? Are houses overpriced ? Is the health care system overburdened ? It must be because of all those pesky people : the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Sarkonak complains , in one of the least densely populated countries on Earth . <p> The specifics of the complaint varies . In the case of labour , the issue would appear to be an excess of supply : too many producers relative to consumers . Whereas with housing and health care , the problem is said to be excess demand : too many consumers relative to producers . The notion that immigrants might be both consumers and producers never seems to come up . <p> But never mind . What do the data say ? Take health care , first . There 's no doubt that Canada 's health care system is plagued by long and lengthening wait times . But that 's been true for decades . <p> The Fraser Institute tracks these from year to year ( see chart ) . Sure enough , it finds in its most recent report that the median total wait time , from referral to a specialist to treatment , has now grown to 30 weeks , three times as long as in 1993 . <p> But it had already grown @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of Justin Trudeau 's government , and to 26 weeks by 2021 , the year before the big immigration surge of the later Trudeau years . ( Population growth from 2016 through 2021 , at an average of 1.15 per cent of population , was well below the post-1945 average of 1.5 per cent , and not a great deal more than the 1 per cent it averaged during the Harper years . ) <p> The problems in the housing market , similarly , long predate the population boom . I can recall seeing stories about the housing market " bubble " in Canada going back two decades . Certainly price increases hit a new gear in 2021-2022 , but there was something else going on at the time , as you may recall , besides the immigration influx : the pandemic , and the massive loosening of fiscal and monetary policy that followed it . When that was unwound , prices began to fall , even as immigration soared . <p> As for wage stagnation : what wage stagnation ? Median hourly wages are up 20 per cent , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ bit after 2021 , but that could as easily be attributed to the sudden unexpected spike in inflation coming out of the pandemic , which outpaced nominal wage gains : by 2024 workers had made up their losses -- again , even as immigration soared . <p> The point is not that high immigration will not have some impact on all of these sectors : of course it will , at least in the short term , as supply adjusts to meet demand and vice versa . That 's especially true in markets as ossified and over-regulated as housing , health care , and labour . <p> Which is surely the point . Immigration and population growth were as high or higher in some years in the 1950s and 1960s , when shortages of housing or health care were unknown and real wages were skyrocketing . <p> The difference ? We had much higher levels of investment then , both generally and in the housing sector in particular . And we had yet to replace prices with politics as the means of allocating scarce resources within the health care system @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , is not that we have too many people : it is that we have too little capital , and too little incentive to make efficient use of the capital we have . Fixing those ought to be our priority , not walling ourself off from the rest of humanity .

How many are you ready to try ? <h> Awareness , acceptance , and action are the recipe for gratitude . <h> Key points <p> Awareness , acceptance , and action is a useful process for developing gratitude . <p> The enemy of these three A 's is resistance , which keeps old defenses as dominant tools for meeting stresses . <p> Old defenses can not be destroyed by attacking them . <p> In the previous post ( Attitude of Gratitude : An Important Recovery Tool ) , I discussed what makes developing an attitude of gratitude difficult . It often requires taking inventory of underlying attitudes such as resentment , cynicism , and pessimism that block our ability to maintain a grateful perspective on life . These deep negative attitudes are frequently adopted during a difficult childhood to protect against painful feelings . However , later in life they can remain as habitual defenses @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ good . <p> Once we become aware that negative attitudes have become our default perspective , we can see how they defeat our efforts at gratitude . It can be maddening to watch our appreciation of beautiful weather , for example , be contaminated by our cynical certainty that climate change is gradually devastating Earth . It 's hard to stay in the present moment when cynicism rushes toward future catastrophes . Why are these attitudes so persistent ? At the risk of anthropomorphizing these defenses ( which only makes sense , since they are an active part of our mental life ) , they resist efforts to eliminate them . From the standpoint of our childhood protective armor , defenses feel they have stood by our side during tough times and continue to be our guardians even when no longer needed . Our willpower generally proves powerless to dislodge such vigorous defenders , even when their presence distorts our view of realities around us . So , how do we divest ourselves of outdated defenses that have literally become part of our identity ? <p> To begin , stop @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ n't like being challenged or told they are bad . They actively resist attacks . The only way to reduce their dominance over us is to develop awareness of the pain they cause . Cynicism , resentment , and pessimism all cause the pain of isolation and disconnection . They all cause the pain of constricting our capacity for enthusiasm . They drain the liveliness out of life . Just as people learn to " think through the drink or drug , " we need to think through the consequences of our negative attitudes . We need to see the pain caused by adopting a cynical perspective , the pain of carrying resentment , the pain of always being so pessimistic we say no to every opportunity . <p> Once we are fully aware of the pain caused by negative defenses at the very moment they are slipping in as our default attitude , a simple cost/benefit analysis makes it clear that negativity is not usually worth the cost . This is where acceptance is a useful tool in two different ways . First , we need to accept that @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ They are present for legitimate reasons , at least initially . Do not shame them but rather acknowledge them in the inventory of yourself . Accept their existence . This does not mean to like them , but rather to recognize their presence . <p> Secondly , accept that these old guardians are inadvertently causing pain in your current life . The more thoroughly aware you become of the pain they cause , the more likely you will become willing to leave them behind . For people in 12-step recovery , this is the essence of step six , perhaps the most critical step for changing your psychology . It is one thing to say you do not want to be cynical anymore , but an entirely different thing to become so sick and tired of the pain caused by cynicism that you become entirely ready to let go of this old protector . Working the sixth step makes room for new possibilities to become available . <p> The process of awareness , then acceptance , reduces our defenses ' resistance to no longer being on center stage and prepares @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . That 's a whole other story . <p> Life never gets easier . Fortunately , psychology is keeping up , uncovering new ways to maintain mental and physical health , and positivity and confidence , through manageable daily habits like these . How many are you ready to try ?

@@127151417 <p> Vid Ingelevics is a visual artist , former educator and now professor emeritus at Toronto Metropolitan University , where he taught in undergraduate and graduate programs . His exhibitions , curatorial endeavours and writings on art and photography have appeared across Canada and in the United States , Europe and Australia . <h> A river runs through it <p> My connection with Toronto 's Port Lands began with a high school summer job at the Smith Transport offices on 150 Commissioners St. , a company where my father worked . I remember the heady mix of fumes rising from the dozens of leaky gas and oil tanks and the sickly sweet odour of soap wafting from the nearby Lever Brothers plant just across the Don River . <p> The Port Lands industrial sector was created in the early 20th century by filling in Toronto 's extensive marshlands that extended from the delta of the river . Years earlier , the Don 's already altered natural course was forced into a 90-degree turn westward through the concrete-lined Keating Channel . <p> A 1964 aerial view of the Gardiner Expressway in @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Keating Channel.Boris Spremo/The Globe and Mail <p> In the decades since , the potential flood risk to hundreds of acres in this area adjacent to downtown Toronto has risen dramatically as climate change has increasingly become a driver of extreme weather . <p> Fifty-six years later , I returned as a photographer to begin work with my colleague , Ryan Walker , on a six-year commission to " document and interpret " the Port Lands Flood Protection Project , one the most ambitious public infrastructure and climate-change adaptation plans in North America . <p> The overwhelming prospect of capturing such a mammoth undertaking led to the idea of collaborating with Ryan , a former student of mine in the Documentary Media program at Toronto Metropolitan University . Together we applied for the commission from Waterfront Toronto . <p> Today , 150 Commissioners St. no longer exists -- the buildings and once-busy truck-loading docks were demolished back in the 1990s .
